result.summary: Pindar confesses he forgot his promised victory song for Agesidamos of Lokris, a boxing winner at Olympia, and pays the debt with interest. He recounts how Herakles founded the Olympic games after defeating Augeas and lists the first winners, then argues that deeds need song to be remembered and praises Agesidamos.

scenes.title: Editor's introductory note
scenes.summary: The editor notes that Pindar delayed this ode and that it was probably sung at an anniversary celebration.

scenes.title: Pindar admits his forgotten debt
scenes.summary: Pindar asks for the winner's name, invokes the Muse and Truth, and promises to repay with interest. He praises Lokris and hopes Agesidamos will thank Ilas as Patroklos thanked Achilles.
scenes.stakes: Pindar's honour, if he is thought to have broken his pledged word to a friend.

scenes.title: Herakles founds the Olympic games
scenes.summary: Herakles kills the sons of Molos, destroys Augeas and his land, and marks out the Altis at Pisa with a feast and sacrifice. He names the Hill of Kronos and founds the games.
scenes.stakes: Herakles seeks the reward Augeas withheld; Augeas faces ruin and death.

scenes.title: The first Olympic winners
scenes.summary: The first victors in each contest are listed, and the evening ends with song under the moon. Pindar will celebrate Zeus's thunder in his own song.

scenes.title: Praise of Agesidamos
scenes.summary: Pindar says unsung deeds are wasted, as an heir is to an old man, and praises Agesidamos's beauty and victory.
scenes.stakes: A man who goes unsung to Hades wastes his toil and wins only brief gladness.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Aphrodite, here unnamed, from her link with Cyprus.

notable_quotes.reason: Terse maxim that achievement requires effort.
Striking simile for why great deeds need song.

analysis.text: The ode links poetry to memory: deeds, like the first Olympic victories, survive only if sung, and Pindar's own lapse shows the poet's debt.
It reflects the Olympic aristocratic culture in which commissioned victory odes honoured winners and cities, here the Lokrians of southern Italy.

fun_facts.text: The editor's note suggests the ode was composed late, perhaps for an anniversary performance, unusually for an epinikion.

language_notes.text: "Payment with usury" means repayment with interest; Pindar promises more than he owes. The wave image suggests the song will rush on and pile up.
Herakles was "foiled" in his fight with Kyknos, son of Ares. The line suggests Lokrians are as formidable in war as they are devoted to the Muse.
Ilas was Agesidamos's trainer. Patroklos was Achilles' close companion, so the line casts the trainer as the one who guided the athlete.
Herakles' quarrel with Augeas was over unpaid wages for cleaning his stables. The "reward for service done" refers to this refusal.
The "sons of Molos" are Kteatos and Eurytos, the Moliones, here called Kleatos and Eurytos, who ambushed Herakles' men in Elis.
"Epeans" are the people of Elis, ruled by Augeas; "guest-betraying" refers to his cheating Herakles.
The Altis was the sacred grove and precinct of Zeus at Olympia; Pisa was the neighbouring district that controlled it.
"The other side of youth" means old age. The comparison is that an heir is a comfort, as a song is for the dead hero.
Ganymede was a beautiful Trojan youth carried off by Zeus to be cupbearer of the gods and made immortal; here beauty is linked to lasting fame.

context_notes.text: The Olympian winner's return home was normally greeted with a victory song. This ode seems to have come too late for that.
The Muse inspires poets, and Truth, daughter of Zeus, here stands for honesty in keeping a promise.
Oinomaos was the king of Pisa, father of Hippodameia, whose legendary chariot race with Pelops is linked to Olympia.
Dirke was a spring near Thebes, Pindar's home city, so the line points to his own place of composition.

literary_notes.text: Pindar shows himself as a forgetful but honourable poet, admitting his debt openly, which wins the reader's sympathy.
The rushing wave sweeping the shingle compares the song's flow with the swift payment of the debt, and implies it will outweigh it.
A short proverb-like remark generalizes from Augeas's fate: opposing stronger powers has no easy escape.
The Fates and Time attend the first games as witnesses, with Time presented as the one who proves truth.
The moon's shining over the precinct and the festal songs give a picture of the first victory celebration, which links to Pindar's own song.
The unsung hero is likened to an old man whose wealth passes to a stranger, which shows that deeds without song are wasted.
